meta.title: Who really said "Military Intelligence is a Contradiction in Terms or an Oxymoron"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not George Carlin. The joke was in print in 1931 — in the war memoir of Field Marshal Haig's own chief of intelligence, Brigadier-General John Charteris.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Military Intelligence is a Contradiction in Terms or an Oxymoron'?
meta.ogDescription: Carlin used it on SNL in 1975. But Haig's intelligence chief John Charteris put it in print in 1931 — about a politician who dismissed his work.

answer.label: Not George Carlin — actually John Charteris
answer.authorDates: 1877–1946 · British brigadier-general and chief of intelligence at BEF General Headquarters, 1915–1918
answer.sourceLine: The line was in print in 1931, in At G.H.Q., the war memoir of Brigadier-General John Charteris — Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig’s own chief of intelligence — who wrote of a visiting Lord Curzon: “I fancy Military Intelligence to him is a contradiction in terms.” Carlin did tell a version of the joke, but the earliest record of it is from November 1974, and his own wording was different: “it’s like Military Intelligence – the words don’t go together, man.”

source.heading: The 1931 memoir

docMeta.dd: Cassell and Company, London, 1931 · viii, 363 pp.

source.excerpt: Curzon did not give much time to Intelligence work. I fancy Military Intelligence to him is a contradiction in terms.
trail: 1931 — Brigadier-General John Charteris publishes At G.H.Q. in London. In the entry dated 5 February 1916, describing Lord Curzon’s visit to headquarters, he writes that “Military Intelligence to him is a contradiction in terms.” The scanned first edition carries the sentence exactly.

1931–1967 — the phrase escapes the book and circulates on its own. Punch reprints it in a review that October; the psychoanalyst Theodor Reik reaches for it in 1963, Shirley Hazzard puts it in a New Yorker story in 1966, and Time uses it in a 1967 film review — a chain documented citation by citation by Quote Investigator.

January 1971 — the joke reaches a mass audience through Doctor Who. In Terror of the Autons, broadcast from 2 January, the Third Doctor tells his companion: “You know Jo, I sometimes think that military intelligence is a contradiction in terms.” That is three years before either comedian is documented using it.

1974–1975 — the comedians arrive. Groucho Marx tosses it at an interviewer in March 1974; a Baton Rouge critic describes Carlin doing the bit that November; and on the Saturday Night Live premiere of 11 October 1975 Carlin delivers the version most people remember: “it’s like Military Intelligence – the words don’t go together, man.”
source.excerptNote: “Curzon” is Lord Curzon, who had come to visit General Headquarters; the surrounding entry is a sketch of his manner during that visit. Quote Investigator had the passage verified on paper at pages 135–136 of the Cassell first edition, and the same wording is legible in the scanned copy linked below.

source.rightsNote: At G.H.Q. was first published in London by Cassell and Company in 1931. Under United States law a work first published in 1931 is still within its copyright term, so the book is treated here as in copyright and only the short passage needed to document the attribution is reproduced. Charteris died in 1946; in his own country the term runs from the author’s death rather than from publication, but the more conservative US position governs this page.

author.name: John Charteris
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Haig’s intelligence chief
author.metaLine: 1877–1946 · British brigadier-general; Haig’s chief of intelligence at GHQ, 1915–1918
author.bio: Charteris was a British Army officer who served as chief of intelligence at British Expeditionary Force General Headquarters from 1915 to 1918, working directly under Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig. In 1931 he published At G.H.Q., assembled from the papers, notes and letters he had kept at the front and rewritten into diary form. Its passing remark about Lord Curzon is now quoted far more widely than anything else he wrote — almost always under someone else’s name.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit instead
misattribution.intro: Two comedians are credited with this line far more often than the soldier who published it — and awkwardly for the fact-checker, both of them really did tell a version of it. They just did so decades later, and in different words.

items.why: Carlin genuinely used the gag. But the earliest record of him doing so is a Baton Rouge review of his act from November 1974, and his best-known telling is the Saturday Night Live premiere of 11 October 1975: “it’s like Military Intelligence – the words don’t go together, man.” That is roughly four decades after Charteris was in print, and it is not the “contradiction in terms” wording pinned to Carlin’s name. Reference works still hand it to him: Wikipedia’s article on the oxymoron presents “military intelligence” as Carlin’s observation.

The credit to Groucho is older than the credit to Carlin: Alan Dershowitz ascribed the line to him in the New York Times in February 1971. Groucho’s own documented use came later still — a March 1974 newspaper item quotes him answering a question about a Pentagon spying ring with “Military intelligence … isn’t that a contradiction in terms?” Both citations are laid out in order by Quote Investigator.

Charteris wrote “contradiction in terms,” and so did everyone through the 1960s. Calling it an oxymoron is a later habit: the earliest instance Quote Investigator locates is a 1973 article in Television Quarterly that names no author at all, followed by a 1976 Portland newspaper piece that pins the oxymoron version on Groucho. If you are quoting the line as “Military Intelligence is an oxymoron,” you are quoting nobody in particular.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke belongs to a professional intelligence officer, not a comedian. Brigadier-General John Charteris wrote it about Lord Curzon in At G.H.Q. (1931), and it was already in circulation through Punch, Time and Doctor Who before either Groucho Marx or George Carlin is documented saying anything like it.

context.heading: A soldier’s joke, not a comedian’s
lead: The line reads today as anti-military sarcasm, which is why it sits so comfortably in a stand-up set. Its author was a career soldier who ran military intelligence for the largest army Britain had ever put in the field. Charteris was Haig’s intelligence chief at General Headquarters from 1915 to 1918, and he set the remark down about Lord Curzon, a politician who had come to visit the front and given his department very little of his time.

That changes the joke. In Carlin’s hands it means the army is stupid. In Charteris’s hands it means something sharper and more particular: that a grandee could not be bothered to take intelligence work seriously, and would have been faintly amused to hear the two words used together. The man being mocked is the visitor, not the service.
context.detailsSummary: One honest caveat about the 1916 date
detailsBody: The entry carrying the line is dated 5 February 1916, but that is the date of the entry, not proof the sentence was written that day. Charteris says so himself in the book’s preface: he “had not kept a formal diary,” and compiled the volume from notes and preserved letters, adding that “where the records were incomplete, I have amplified them by my recollections.” He signs that preface from Ecclefechan and dates it 1 January 1931.

So the safe claim is the one this page makes: the sentence is documented in print in 1931, and Quote Investigator — which examined the same book on paper — treats Charteris as the earliest known source while explicitly flagging that the 1916 entry may have been amplified later. Nothing found so far puts the joke in anyone else’s mouth before him.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes John Charteris is the earliest documented source, quoting At G.H.Q. (1931): "Curzon did not give much time to Intelligence work. I fancy Military Intelligence to him is a contradiction in terms", verified on paper at pages 135 and 136; and documents Punch (Oct 1931), Theodor Reik (1963), Shirley Hazzard in The New Yorker (1966), Time (1967), Doctor Who (Jan 1971), Dershowitz crediting Groucho in the NYT (Feb 1971), Television Quarterly using 'oxymoron' (1973), Groucho's own March 1974 interview quip, a Nov 1974 Baton Rouge review of Carlin, Carlin on SNL (1975), and a 1976 Oregonian piece crediting the oxymoron version to Groucho.

The scanned 1931 first edition of At G.H.Q. contains, in the entry dated February 5 within the 1916 section, the words "Curzon did not give much time to Intelligence work. I fancy Military Intelligence to him is a contradiction in terms."; the printed page numbers in the surrounding run place it on pages 135-136, matching QI's paper verification. Its preface states Charteris "had not kept a formal diary", that he compiled the volume from notes and preserved letters, that "where the records were incomplete, I have amplified them by my recollections", and it is signed from Ecclefechan and dated 1.1.31.

John Charteris lived 1877-1946, held the rank of Brigadier-General, served as Chief of Intelligence at British Expeditionary Force General Headquarters from 1915 to 1918 under Field Marshal Douglas Haig, and his 1931 memoir At G.H.Q. consisted of papers, notes and letters re-written into diary form because he had not kept a diary at the time. The page also notes he is cited by Quote Investigator as the source of the saying.
At G.H.Q. by Charteris, John, 1877-1946, was published by Cassell, London, in 1931, viii + 363 pages.

On the Saturday Night Live premiere of 11 October 1975, George Carlin said: "The term Jumbo Shrimp has always amazed me. What is a Jumbo Shrimp? I mean, it's like Military Intelligence - the words don't go together, man."

Wikiquote's Third Doctor page records, under the serial Terror of the Autons [8.1] with broadcast dates 2-23 January 1971, the line "You know Jo, I sometimes think that military intelligence is a contradiction in terms."
Terror of the Autons was written by Robert Holmes and originally broadcast from 2 to 23 January 1971 as the first serial of Doctor Who season 8.

Wikipedia's Oxymoron article presents 'military intelligence' as George Carlin's observation, stating that examples popularized by comedian George Carlin in 1975 include 'military intelligence', and naming no earlier originator.

NEGATIVE CHECK (link deliberately not used on the page): George Carlin's Wikiquote page lists 'military intelligence' or 'jumbo shrimp' among his sourced, disputed or misattributed quotes. Fetched and confirmed absent - Wikiquote does not corroborate the popular Carlin credit in any section.
